\chapter{Saying, and Thinking}
\label{ch:ta-saying-and-thinking}
\hlchaptermodality{77}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can report what was said and give an opinion, by putting a whole sentence inside another.}

Complete TA-C77-opinion and give an opinion about two different things.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sol]{\ta{சொல்} (sol) — to say, to tell}

\label{lesson:TA-C77-say}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}}. Then offer somebody milk or tea.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சொல்}}
\textbf{\ta{சொல்}} (\emph{sol}) — \textquotedblleft{}to say, to tell\textquotedblright{}.

You have been using this verb since chapter eight without being told its name. \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}} — \textquotedblleft{}please tell me\textquotedblright{} — is \ta{சொல்} with the respectful ending you met in the same chapter.

Now it stands on its own, the way \ta{போ} and \ta{வா} and \ta{சாப்பிடு} do.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{சொல்}} — say it
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}} — please say it
\end{quote}

\ta{சொல்} also means \emph{a word}. The same three letters name the thing and the act, and no Tamil speaker finds that odd: a word is what saying produces.

You will need this verb for the next lesson, because Tamil has a particular way of handing somebody else's words to it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A verb you have been saying since chapter eight, now yours to use.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sol}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sol}, then \emph{solluṅgaḷ} — the bare verb, then the polite one
  \item \emph{Notice:} the second meaning, \emph{a word}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}}, then offer \emph{pāl alladu tēnīr?}, then say \emph{sol}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{nāṉ uḷḷē varalāmā?}, \emph{mutalil} and \emph{siri} — three distances back — then quote one of them with \ta{என்று}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word you already knew is this verb wearing a polite ending? (\textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eṉṟu]{\ta{என்று} (eṉṟu) — the end of a quotation}

\label{lesson:TA-C77-quotative}



\begin{quote}
Offer somebody a choice of two drinks. Then say the verb \emph{to say}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: the quotation carries its own closing word}]
English opens a quotation with \emph{that} or with a comma. Tamil closes it, with \textbf{\ta{என்று}}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}\ta{சரி}\textquotedblright{} \ta{என்று} \ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{} eṉṟu solluṅgaḷ.} — 'Say \textquotedblleft{}okay\textquotedblright{}.'
\end{quote}

The words being reported come first, whole and unchanged. \textbf{\ta{என்று}} then marks where they end, and the verb of saying comes last, where every Tamil verb goes.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}\ta{பால்} \ta{வேண்டும்}\textquotedblright{} \ta{என்று} \ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
'Say \textquotedblleft{}I want milk\textquotedblright{}.'
\end{quote}

\ta{என்று} is itself made from an old verb meaning \emph{to say}, so what you are doing is saying that something was said. Two sayings, one sentence — and that is why nothing needs to be added at the front.

Everyday speech shortens it to \textbf{-\ta{ன்னு}}, stuck straight onto the quotation: \emph{sari-ṉṉu solluṅgaḷ}. You will hear that far more often than the full word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to put a whole sentence inside another one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{eṉṟu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{} eṉṟu solluṅgaḷ}
  \item \emph{Build:} \emph{\textquotedblleft{}pāl vēṇḍum\textquotedblright{} eṉṟu solluṅgaḷ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} offer \emph{pāl alladu tēnīr?}, then say \emph{sol}, then say the whole quoted line
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{āṉāl}, \emph{vēṇḍukōḷ} and \emph{aḻu} — three distances back — then quote one of them with \ta{என்று}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \ta{என்று} stand — before the quoted words or after them? (\textbf{After. It closes them, and the verb follows.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sol]{\ta{சொல்} — a sign on both sides of one letter}

\label{lesson:TA-W32-read-sol}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: say the verb \emph{to say}, then close a quotation with \ta{என்று}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{சொல்} — two letters, and a sign that surrounds one}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{சொ}} & \emph{so} & \ta{ச} with the \textbf{\ta{ொ}} sign \\
\textbf{\ta{ல்}} & \emph{l} & \ta{ல} with a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{சொ} · \ta{ல்} $\to$ \ta{சொல்}}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{\ta{ொ}} sign is the one you first met inside \textbf{\ta{சொல்லுங்கள்}} in chapter eight, and it is unusual: it puts one piece \textbf{before} its letter and another \textbf{after} it. The letter sits in the middle of its own vowel.

Compare it with \textbf{\ta{ோ}} in \textbf{\ta{போ}}, which does the same thing for the long \emph{ō}. Tamil has a small family of signs that wrap around, and both of them are in words you already say.

The word ends the way \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}} did, on a \ta{ல்} carrying a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{சொ}} — then \textbf{\ta{ல்}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{சொல்}}, then \textbf{\ta{போ}} — two wrapping signs, one short and one long
  \item \emph{Point to:} the two halves of the \ta{ொ} sign, and the letter caught between them
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sol}, then say \emph{\textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{} eṉṟu solluṅgaḷ}, then read \textbf{\ta{சொல்}}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{alladu}, \emph{aṉumati} and \emph{iṉṟu} — three distances back — then quote one of them with \ta{என்று}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is unusual about the \ta{ொ} sign? (\textbf{It wraps around its letter — part before, part after.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… eṉṟu niṉaikkiṟēṉ]{… \ta{என்று} \ta{நினைக்கிறேன்} — I think that …}

\label{lesson:TA-C77-opinion}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{சொல்}}. Then say: 'Say \textquotedblleft{}okay\textquotedblright{}.'
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: what \ta{என்று} hands to \ta{நினை}}
\textbf{\ta{நினை}} (\emph{ninai}) has been in the book since chapter thirty-three: \textquotedblleft{}to think\textquotedblright{}. Until now it had nothing to think \textbf{about}, because a thought is a whole sentence and nothing could carry one.

\ta{என்று} carries one.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{இது} \ta{நல்ல} \ta{வீடு} \ta{என்று} \ta{நினைக்கிறேன்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{idu nalla vīḍu eṉṟu niṉaikkiṟēṉ.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}I think this is a good house.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The opinion comes first and stands whole — \textbf{\ta{இது} \ta{நல்ல} \ta{வீடு}}, a sentence you could say on its own. \ta{என்று} closes it. Then the verb, built the way \ta{பேசுகிறேன்} was in chapter five: \ta{நினை}, the middle piece for \emph{now}, and \textbf{-\ta{ஏன்}} for \emph{I}.

Swap the front half for anything you can say:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{இது} \ta{சிறிய} \ta{கடை} \ta{என்று} \ta{நினைக்கிறேன்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
An opinion, which is the first thing here that is yours rather than a fact.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{niṉaikkiṟēṉ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{idu nalla vīḍu eṉṟu niṉaikkiṟēṉ}
  \item \emph{Swap:} put \emph{idu siṟiya kaḍai} in the front half and say the whole thing
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{} eṉṟu solluṅgaḷ}, then read \textbf{\ta{சொல்}}, then give your opinion
  \item \emph{Return to:} read \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}}, say \emph{tayakkam} and say \emph{nēṟṟu} — three distances back — then quote one of them with \ta{என்று}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What stands between your opinion and the verb \ta{நினைக்கிறேன்}? (\textbf{\ta{என்று}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
